I was standing behind a barn with a few friends smoking weed late at night in the dead of winter my freshmen year of college, when we heard a sliding door open about ten feet away. We all froze as a guy stepped out onto his first-floor porch to smoke a cigarette. We hoped he wouldn't see us, because we were young and naïve, but he did notice, and told us something none of us will ever forget: "Don't mind me, I don't give a shit". It made us realize that what other people do largely doesn't affect us, and so we don't need to care about it. Eight years later (almost nine, holy shit), I see people doing things that an uptight person might whine about, but you know what? I don't give a shit. They're doing what they like, and it doesn't hurt anyone, so why bother wasting the energy to complain about it?

I think I'm a more zen person now, because of that night. It's what I think is the most important thing I learned in college.

I came here to post something similar. When I was 16, my dad and I went on a trip together. I was very self-conscious, and especially cringed at his attempts to speak the local language, which I spoke fluently (I was too much of a teenager to understand that the locals mostly appreciated that he made the effort). Over dinner, he finally said, "you need to stop worrying what people think about you. People are so wrapped up in themselves and their own shit, they mostly barely even notice you and yours." Best advice I've ever gotten, and definitely helped me survive college.

I'm a woman....but this advice can still apply.
